keyVerseText: And Baalhanan the son of Achbor died, and Hadar reigned in his stead: and the name of his city was Pau; and his wife's name was Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred, the daughter of Mezahab. Hadar, Pau: or, Hadad, Pai: after his death was an Aristocracy
rootMeaning: The root of מַטְרֵד (Maṭrêd) comes from the Hebrew root טָרַד (ṭârad), which carries the idea of driving forward or pursuing continuously. This root suggests a sense of propulsion or persistent movement. Thus, the name Maṭrêd, meaning "pushing forward," reflects an active, forward-driving force rather than a passive state, which adds a dynamic nuance beyond a simple proper noun.
usageInScripture: The word מַטְרֵד appears only twice in Scripture, both times as a proper name referring to a woman, the daughter of Mezahab and mother of Mehetabel, who was the wife of Hadar (Hadad), king of Edom. Its consistent translation as "of Matred" indicates that the term functions strictly as a personal name rather than a common noun or verb. This limited usage highlights its role in genealogical and historical records rather than narrative or poetic contexts.
theologicalSignificance: Though מַטְרֵד is a proper name, understanding its root meaning enriches our appreciation of biblical names as carriers of character or destiny. The notion of "pushing forward" resonates with the biblical theme of God’s providential guidance and the forward movement of His redemptive plan through generations. As a mother-in-law in the Edomite royal line, Matred’s name reminds believers that God’s sovereign purposes advance through ordinary people and family lines, underscoring His faithfulness in history. This invites reflection on how God uses all persons, named and unnamed, to fulfill His covenant promises ultimately realized in Christ.
keyVerseReflection: Genesis 36:39 records that Hadar, king of Edom, was married to Mehetabel, the daughter of Matred. The mention of Matred here anchors Hadar’s lineage and royal legitimacy. The word מַטְרֵד as a name conveys more than identity; it symbolizes a forward-driving legacy within Edom’s history. This reminds readers that behind every biblical figure is a family story that contributes to God’s unfolding plan, encouraging faith in God’s sovereign orchestration even in seemingly peripheral details.
